subtype: Refusing with no and pulling away [Expressing]
passage: At Ayesha's mother-in-law's lunch in Hyderabad, Keerthana, two, pushed the spoon of dal away and turned her face to the wall. "No." Ayesha put the spoon down. "Okay, later." A visiting aunt leaned in for a cheek pinch. Keerthana pulled back and gripped her mother's kurta. "She would like a wave today," said Ayesha, and the aunt smiled and waved. Keerthana waved back, still holding on.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do when the spoon of dal came near?
qa.a: She pushed the spoon away, turned her face to the wall and said no.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been feeling when she pulled back from the aunt, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: She seems to feel that she does not want to be touched right now, since she gripped her mother. She might also have been tired or full of the lunch.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that teaches something useful?
qa.a: Ayesha accepted the small refusals and gave the aunt another way to be friendly, which shows Keerthana that her body is hers.

qa.q: How might the aunt feel about the refusal?
qa.a: She may feel a bit surprised, but a warm wave can let her connect without offence.

grounding: A toddler refuses with no and pulling away, and adults respect small refusals about touch and food where safe.

passage:
"No!" Lokesh pushed the bowl across the tray.
"All done with the rice?" asked Shankar.
"No, no." He turned his head.
"Okay. Bowl goes away. Hungry later, you tell me."
His grandmother leaned in. "A kiss, Lokesh?"
Lokesh hid behind Shankar's arm.
"Maybe a wave," said Shankar. Lokesh peeked out and waved. Shankar squeezed his hand.

qa.q: What did Lokesh push away first?
qa.a: He pushed the bowl of rice across the tray.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's hiding behind Shankar's arm suggest, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: It suggests he does not want a kiss right now but still feels safe near Shankar. It could also mean he is sleepy or in a mood.

qa.q: What could Shankar do if Lokesh is hungry later?
qa.a: Shankar can offer the food again calmly without making a fuss about the earlier refusal.

qa.q: How might the grandmother see Lokesh's refusal?
qa.a: She may feel a little sad at first, but a wave from him lets her feel his affection in a way he is comfortable with.

grounding: A toddler refuses food and touch, and adults respect small refusals where safe.

subtype: Refusing with no and pulling away [Expressing]
passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. After lunch, when I reached to wipe Raghav's face, he pulled his head back and said, "No!" and pushed my hand away. I stopped. "Do you want to wipe it yourself?" I held out the cloth. He took it and rubbed his cheeks, very pleased with himself. I'll ask first with him from now on. Ayesha, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Ayesha hold out to Raghav?
qa.a: The cloth.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he pulled away and said "No!"?
qa.a: He didn't want someone else touching his face and wanted to do it himself; he felt proud once he could.

qa.q: Why was it a good idea for Ayesha to stop and offer the cloth?
qa.a: It respected his refusal about his own body while still getting his face clean.

qa.q: What would change if Ayesha had held his head and wiped anyway?
qa.a: Raghav would learn that his "no" about his body doesn't count, and he'd likely struggle more.

grounding: A teacher respects a toddler's refusal of face-wiping and offers him the cloth, teaching that his body is his.

passage:
At the village wedding, an aunt swooped down on Karthik. "Such fat cheeks!" she said, and pinched one.
Karthik pulled away sharply. "No!" He buried his face in his mother's lap.
"He doesn't want that," said Vinita, his mother, gently. "Maybe he'll wave instead?"
The aunt blinked, then smiled and stepped back. After a moment, Karthik lifted one hand and gave her a small wave.

qa.q: What did the aunt pinch?
qa.a: Karthik's cheek.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he pulled away and said "No!"?
qa.a: He was uncomfortable and upset at being pinched, and wanted to protect himself.

qa.q: Which of Vinita's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Gently saying he didn't want that and suggesting a wave worked, because it respected his refusal and still let him greet the aunt.

qa.q: How might the aunt feel when Vinita speaks up?
qa.a: The aunt might feel a little surprised, but she seems to accept it, smiling and stepping back.

grounding: A mother backs her toddler's refusal of a cheek pinch and offers another way to greet, teaching body autonomy.

passage:
At dinner in the Singapore flat, Leila, Mei's nanny, held out another spoonful of rice. Mei turned her head away and pushed the spoon with her hand. "No."
Leila put the spoon down. "All done? Okay."
Mei's mother frowned. "She's barely eaten."
"She ate her fish and her beans," Leila said. "She's saying she's full." Mei climbed down and went off happily to her blocks.

qa.q: What had Mei eaten, according to Leila?
qa.a: Her fish and her beans.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling when she pushed the spoon away?
qa.a: She was likely full and wanted to stop; she seemed content as she went off to her blocks.

qa.q: Which choice of Leila's worked, and why?
qa.a: Accepting "no" and putting the spoon down worked, because Mei had eaten a fair amount and learned her refusal was respected.

qa.q: How does Mei's mother see the refusal?
qa.a: She worries Mei hasn't eaten enough, rather than seeing a full child saying no.

grounding: A nanny respects a toddler's "no" to more food, teaching that the child's body signals count.

passage:
I'm Chetan, and my little sister Shreya is two. When Mama's friend visited, he bent down to pinch her cheek.
Shreya turned her face away and pushed his hand with both of hers. “No!”
“Arre, just a small pinch,” he said.
Mummy said, “She doesn't want it, and that's okay. Maybe a high five?” Shreya held up her hand.
At dinner she pushed her bowl away. “No more.” Mummy took the bowl away.

qa.q: How old is Shreya?
qa.a: Shreya is two.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she turned away and pushed the hand?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable with the cheek pinch and did not want to be touched, and her push and "No!" clearly said so.

qa.q: Why was Mummy right to back Shreya's "No"?
qa.a: Respecting her small refusals about touch and food, where it is safe, teaches Shreya that her body belongs to her.

qa.q: How did Mama's friend react to Shreya pushing his hand?
qa.a: He seemed to brush it off, saying it was just a small pinch.

grounding: It shows a toddler refusing touch and food by saying no and pushing away, and an adult respecting those refusals.
